text:
Help me write an announcement to our staff. I'm the COO of a credit union with 7 branches. We're closing the Maple Street and Route 9 branches on March 31 and moving the people who work there to a new member phone and chat center.

Facts:
- The two branches have 14 staff between them. Every one of them is offered a job in the phone and chat center at the same pay or higher.
- Visits to those two branches fell 44% over the last three years. Phone and chat contacts across the credit union went up 60%.
- Members calling us now wait an average of 9 minutes on hold.
- The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. The branches were open 9 to 5. Shifts will rotate.
- Staff in the center can work from home two days a week after 90 days of training.
- Anyone who doesn't take the new role gets 2 weeks of pay for every year they've worked here.

I want the announcement to say that this change will make everyone's job better. About 400 words, sent by email from me.

Before I draft, there's one decision for you and a few facts only you have.

**The decision: "this change will make everyone's job better"**

Your facts support part of that line, but not all of it.

- **What the facts support:** Nobody loses a job. Nobody's pay goes down, and some people's goes up. Staff can work from home two days a week once training is done. They'll be working where members actually are now: phone and chat contacts are up 60%, and callers wait 9 minutes on hold.
- **What they don't support:** These staff now work 9 to 5. The center is open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. with rotating shifts, so most of them will probably work some early or late hours they don't work today. They also lose face-to-face work with members, and some may have chosen branch work for exactly that reason. The 14 people reading this will see that straight away. If the email says "better for everyone," they'll stop trusting the rest of it, including the parts that really are good news.
- **What I'd suggest saying instead:** Every one of you keeps a job at the same pay or more, and you'll be doing work members are waiting for. The change also asks something of you: different hours, rotating shifts and a new kind of work. Here's what we're doing to make that work for you.

I'd write that version, and I'd still make the positive case clearly. It's your call, though. If you want the "better for everyone" version, I'll write that instead.

**Questions (the most important first)**

1. **Shifts.** How long is a shift, and how often will someone work past 5 p.m. or start at 8 a.m.? Is there extra pay for evening shifts, and can staff ask for set hours? This is the first thing everyone will ask about.
2. **Location.** Where is the center? Will the commute be longer for Maple Street or Route 9 staff?
3. **Deadlines and severance terms.** When do staff have to decide? When does training start? Is the severance payment capped, or is there a minimum? Do benefits continue? Can someone accept the role and change their mind during training?
4. **Who's affected and who's been told.** Have the 14 staff already heard this from their managers in person, or is this email how they find out? It goes to all staff, so people at the other five branches will be wondering whether their branch is next. Is there anything you can honestly tell them?
5. **Support.** Is the 90 days of training paid? Is there a named contact for questions, and are there one-on-one meetings planned?
6. **Anything they'll find out anyway.** Is there a cost, a limit or a bit of history this email leaves out that staff know or will learn? For example, past closures, or how members of those two branches will be told.

Answer whichever you can. Where you don't know, I'll leave it out rather than guess.

You're right, "better for everyone" goes too far. Write the version that says what's true.

1. I don't know shift length, how often people would work early or late, or whether there's evening pay. I can't promise anyone 9 to 5. Staff with the most years here pick shifts first.
2. The center is at our main office on Elm Avenue. I don't know how commutes compare.
3. Written offers go out by February 14, and decisions are due March 1. Anyone who takes the new role and wants out within 6 months can still get the severance. I don't know the training start date, whether there's a cap or minimum on severance, or about benefits.
4. I don't know who's been told yet, or what I can say to the other five branches.
5. Anyone who wants a one-on-one meeting with HR can have one. I don't know whether training is paid or who the named contact is.
6. Our current phone team lost about 30% of its people last year. Also, center pay starts $1.50 an hour above current teller pay. And the two branches can't stay open. That's decided.

For the sign-off: I'm Rachel Greene, COO, Northfield Community Credit Union.

I've kept the closure firm, given the reasons once, and put the harder parts (the hours and the phone team's 30% turnover) right next to the strongest answer you have: staff can try the new role and still leave with full severance.

<final_document>
**Subject: Maple Street and Route 9 branches closing March 31**

To all Northfield staff,

I'm writing to share a decision that directly affects many of you. On March 31, we will close our Maple Street and Route 9 branches. Every one of the 14 people who work at those branches will be offered a job in a new member phone and chat center at our main office on Elm Avenue, at the same pay or higher.

**Why we're doing this.** Over the last three years, visits to those two branches fell 44%. Over the same period, phone and chat contacts across the credit union rose 60%. Members who call us today wait an average of 9 minutes on hold. Our members have changed how they reach us, and right now we aren't keeping up. The decision to close the two branches is final.

**What the new role offers.** Pay in the center starts at $1.50 an hour above current teller pay. After 90 days of training, center staff can work from home two days a week. You'll also be helping members who are waiting for help right now.

**What it asks of you.** The center is open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, and shifts will rotate. I can't promise anyone 9-to-5 hours. Staff with the most years here will pick their shifts first. I don't have shift lengths or schedules yet. Phone and chat work is also different from branch work, and I won't pretend otherwise: our current phone team lost about 30% of its people last year. I take that number seriously.

**Your choice and your timeline.**
- Written offers go out by February 14.
- Decisions are due March 1.
- If you decide not to take the new role, you'll receive two weeks of pay for every year you've worked here.
- If you take the role and decide within six months that it isn't right for you, you can still leave with the same severance.

That last point matters to me. I'd rather you try the role knowing you can leave than turn it down because you're unsure.

If you'd like to talk this through privately, you can book a one-on-one meeting with HR. Bring your questions, and tell them what would make this a job you'd want to stay in.

You've built strong relationships with members at Maple Street and Route 9, and closing those branches isn't easy for any of us. I hope many of you will bring that experience to the center, where members need it.

Rachel Greene
Chief Operating Officer
Northfield Community Credit Union
</final_document>

**Before you send it:**

- **Missing details.** Staff will ask about shift length, evening pay, whether training is paid, when training starts, benefits, and severance caps or minimums. They have to decide by March 1. I haven't promised a date for any of these, but if you can get answers before February 14, add them to the offer letters.
- **Tell the 14 staff first.** It's still undecided who has heard. If possible, have managers tell the Maple Street and Route 9 staff in person before this email goes to everyone.
- **The other five branches.** The email says nothing to staff at the other branches, so they'll likely wonder whether they're next. Once you know what you can honestly tell them, a single sentence would help.
- **Check two lines are true for you.** "I take that number seriously" and "I'd rather you try the role…" are written in your voice, but they aren't from the facts you gave me. Keep them only if they're true for you. The first will lead staff to expect some action on turnover.
